corpus_definition: To surprise or frighten someone suddenly.

forms.note: There is no common learner noun. Startle as a noun (the startle response) is a technical word used by doctors and scientists.

forms.definition: to surprise or frighten someone suddenly so that they jump
forms.example: Sorry, I didn't mean to startle you when I opened the door.

syn.note: Easy, general word; startle adds the idea of a sudden small shock.
Frighten is about fear; startle is short and sudden, and the fear goes quickly.
Easy, everyday phrase with the same meaning.
Shock is usually stronger and lasts longer.
Alarm means to make someone worried that something bad will happen.

ant.note: To make someone feel quiet and relaxed again.

forms.definition: suddenly surprised or a little frightened
forms.example: The startled cat ran under the bed.

syn.note: Easy word; startled adds a sudden small jump of fear.
Alarmed means worried that something bad will happen.
Shocked is usually stronger and about something bad.
Frightened is about fear that can last a long time.

ant.note: Relaxed and not worried or surprised.

forms.definition: very surprising and unexpected
forms.example: The report showed some startling facts about water use in the city.

syn.note: Easy word, very close; startling is a little stronger.
Very surprising, often about something good or impressive.
Surprising in a bad or upsetting way.

ant.note: Expected; not surprising at all.

forms.definition: in a very surprising way
forms.example: The young singer has a startlingly beautiful voice.

syn.note: Easy word, very close in meaning.
Usually about something good or impressive.
In a way that people notice because it is unusual.

context.text: A loud firework startled the children in the park in Navruz week. One startled boy dropped his ice cream, and his sister laughed in a startlingly loud voice.

reviewer_note: Noun 'startle' is technical only, so no_form with a note; startled and startling are both participial adjectives in this meaning.

corpus_definition: To suffer or die because you have no food.

forms.definition: suffering or death caused by having no food for a long time
forms.example: Many people died of starvation during the war.

syn.note: Easy word; hunger can be small, but starvation is very serious.
A famine is a time when a whole region has no food.
Being ill because you do not eat enough good food.

forms.definition: to suffer or die because you have no food
forms.example: Without help, these animals will starve this winter.

syn.note: Easy phrase; go hungry is less serious than starve.
Easy phrase for the most serious case.
To fast is to choose not to eat, for example in Ramadan; starving is not a choice.

ant.note: To give food to a person or animal.

forms.definition: suffering or dying because there is no food
forms.example: The charity sends rice to starving families.
forms.note: In informal English, 'I'm starving' just means 'I'm very hungry'.

syn.note: Easy word, but much weaker than starving.
Very hungry; used mostly in the informal sense.
Not given enough food for a long time.

ant.note: Having plenty of good food.
Easy word: you have eaten enough.

forms.definition: weak or ill because of having no food
forms.example: The starved dog was too weak to stand.
forms.note: Also used as 'starved of' something: 'starved of love'.
There is no adverb made from starve.

context.text: In the cold winter, many birds starve because the ground is frozen. My grandmother in Nukus always puts bread outside for the starving birds. She says nobody should die of starvation.

reviewer_note: Informal 'I'm starving' (very hungry) covered in a note, not as a separate entry.

corpus_definition: To control the direction of a vehicle like a car or boat.

forms.definition: the parts of a car or boat that control its direction
forms.example: The steering on this old car is very heavy.

syn.note: How easy a car is to control when you drive it.

forms.definition: to control the direction a car, boat or bike goes
forms.example: He steered the car slowly into the narrow street.

syn.note: Drive is the whole action; steer is only about choosing the direction.
To move something carefully in the right direction.
To show or control where something goes.
To find the way, especially on a boat or plane.
Easy word: to change direction.

forms.note: There is no common adjective made from steer; steerable is rare and technical.
There is no adverb made from steer.

context.text: My father taught me to steer a boat on Charvak Lake. The steering was hard at first, but now I can steer it easily.

reviewer_note: The noun steer (a young bull) is a different word with the same spelling; steering wheel is a compound and left out.

corpus_definition: The thin part of a plant that holds the leaves.

forms.definition: the long thin part of a plant that holds the leaves or flowers
forms.example: Cut the stem of each rose before you put it in water.

syn.note: Very close; stalk is often used for vegetables and thicker plants.
A branch grows out of the trunk of a tree.
The thick main part of a tree.

forms.definition: to come from or be caused by something
forms.example: Many of his problems stem from a lack of sleep.
forms.note: Belongs to stem = come from (stem from), not the part of a plant. Another verb meaning is 'to stop a flow': stem the bleeding.
There is no adjective made from stem; long-stemmed is a compound.
There is no adverb made from stem.

context.text: My mother grows tulips in our garden in Fergana. This spring one flower had a very long stem, so she put it in a vase on the table.

reviewer_note: Only one existing form in this meaning; verb stem (stem from) is a different meaning, marked other_meaning.

corpus_definition: A person whose job is to serve passengers on a plane.

forms.definition: a man whose job is to look after passengers on a plane or ship
forms.example: The steward showed us where to put our bags.
forms.note: Today people usually say 'flight attendant' for both men and women.

syn.note: The modern word used for men and women.
The whole team that works with passengers on a plane.
A person whose job is to help people in a public place.

ant.note: The steward serves; the passenger is served.

forms.definition: the careful management and protection of something important
forms.example: The museum is under the stewardship of a new director.
forms.note: Belongs to steward = a person who manages or looks after property or land, not plane staff. Formal.

forms.definition: to help control the crowd at a public event
forms.example: Volunteers will steward the marathon on Sunday.
forms.note: Belongs to steward = a person who helps organize a race or concert, not plane staff. Mostly British.
There is no adjective made from steward.
There is no adverb made from steward.

people.definition: a woman whose job is to look after passengers on a plane
people.example: The stewardess brought us blankets during the night flight.
people.note: Old-fashioned; most people now say 'flight attendant'.

context.text: On our flight from Tashkent to Istanbul, a friendly steward brought us tea. Later a stewardess helped my little brother with his seatbelt.

reviewer_note: Headword is a person noun, so it stays in the noun slot (rule 6); -ess is not in the affix table, so no affix claimed for stewardess.

forms.definition: the state of being hard to bend or move
forms.example: Gentle exercise can help with stiffness in your knees.

syn.note: More formal; often about materials.
Often about muscles that feel tight.
Easy word; stiffness can come with pain, but is not the same.

ant.note: Being able to bend easily.

forms.definition: to become hard to bend or move
forms.example: My fingers stiffen when it is very cold outside.

syn.note: To become hard; used for materials more than for the body.
To make your muscles tight, often because you are nervous.
To become tight.

ant.note: To let your muscles become soft and loose.
To become softer.
To become less tight.

forms.definition: hard to bend, move or turn
forms.example: My legs were stiff after the long bus journey.

syn.note: Very hard and not able to bend at all; often about materials.
Easy word; hard is about not being soft.
Firm is not soft, but still a little flexible.
Often about muscles that do not feel loose.
Not able to bend; also used about people and rules.

ant.note: Able to bend easily.
Easy word: not hard.
Able to bend and move easily, often about the body.

forms.definition: in a way that is not smooth because your body is hard to move
forms.example: After the football match he walked stiffly to the car.
forms.note: Also means 'in an unfriendly, formal way': she smiled stiffly.

syn.note: Without bending at all.
In a way that is not easy or natural.

ant.note: Easily and without stopping or problems.

context.text: After working at the computer all day, my neck is often stiff. My doctor in Tashkent says the stiffness comes from sitting too long. When I stand up, I walk stiffly for a few minutes.

reviewer_note: Stiffen uses -en, which is not in the affix table, so no affix is claimed for it.

corpus_definition: To fix cloth using a needle and thread.

forms.definition: one short line of thread that goes through cloth
forms.example: The doctor needed six stitches to close the cut.
forms.note: Also a sudden pain in your side when you run: 'I've got a stitch.'

syn.note: A round shape made by thread or string.
Medical word for a stitch that closes a cut.

forms.definition: a row of short lines of thread in cloth
forms.example: The stitching on this bag is very strong.

syn.note: Sewing is the activity; stitching is often the lines you can see.
Sewing or embroidery done as a hobby or art.

forms.definition: to sew cloth with a needle and thread
forms.example: Can you stitch this button back onto my coat?

syn.note: Easy word with almost the same meaning.
To repair something that is broken or torn.
General word for fixing anything.

ant.note: To take out the thread from something that was sewn. Mostly British.

forms.note: There is no common adjective made from stitch; people say hand-stitched or hand-sewn.
There is no adverb made from stitch.

context.text: My grandmother in Bukhara can stitch beautiful suzani. Every stitch is very small, and the stitching takes many months to finish.

reviewer_note: Noun stitch (pain in your side) mentioned in a note on the conversion noun; hand-stitched is a compound and left out.

corpus_definition: To pull or push something too hard until it hurts.

forms.definition: an injury to a muscle from pulling it too hard
forms.example: The footballer has a strain in his leg and cannot play.
forms.note: Strain also means worry or pressure: 'the strain of exams'.

syn.note: General word for any damage to the body.
A sprain is damage to a joint, like an ankle; a strain is to a muscle.
Informal: 'a pull in my leg' means a strained muscle.

forms.definition: to hurt a part of your body by using it too hard
forms.example: Bend your knees so you don't strain your back.

syn.note: Easy and common: pull a muscle.
General word for hurting a part of the body.
Easy word for causing pain.
To use something too much without rest.

ant.note: To let your muscles rest and become loose.
Easy word: to stop using something so it gets better.

forms.definition: hurt because it was used or pulled too hard
forms.example: She has a strained muscle in her shoulder.
forms.note: Strained also means 'not relaxed or natural': a strained smile.

syn.note: Easy and common: a pulled muscle.
General word for hurt.
Painful, but not always injured.

forms.note: There is no common adverb in this meaning.

people.definition: a kitchen tool with small holes for separating liquid from food
people.example: Pour the pasta into the strainer.
people.note: Belongs to strain = pour liquid through something with small holes, not hurting a muscle.

context.text: My brother strained his back carrying a heavy carpet up the stairs. The doctor said it was a small strain and he should rest for a week.

reviewer_note: Strenuous looks similar but is not from strain, so it is left out; strain = pressure/worry covered in notes.

corpus_definition: A careful plan made to reach a specific goal.

forms.definition: a careful plan for reaching a goal
forms.example: Our strategy is to study a little every day before the exam.

syn.note: Easy, general word; a strategy is a bigger, longer plan.
A way of dealing with a problem.
A tactic is one small step; a strategy is the whole plan.
A plan; in American English it can sound dishonest.
A set of rules or ideas, usually of a government or company.

forms.definition: to make careful plans to reach a goal
forms.example: The team met to strategize before the final match.
forms.note: Mainly American English; British spelling: strategise.

syn.note: Easy, everyday word with almost the same meaning.

ant.note: To do something without planning it first.

forms.definition: part of a careful plan to reach a goal
forms.example: Opening a shop near the bazaar was a strategic decision.

syn.note: Easy word: decided before.
About small steps, not the whole plan.
Planned carefully, sometimes in a cold way.

ant.note: Done without thinking about it before.

forms.definition: in a way that is part of a careful plan
forms.example: The new hotel is strategically placed near the airport.

syn.note: About small steps rather than the whole plan.
Easy word, more general.

ant.note: Without any plan or order.

people.definition: a person who is skilled at making careful plans
people.example: The company hired a strategist to help it grow.

context.text: Our football coach in Samarkand has a clear strategy for every game. He makes strategic changes at half-time, and the players are strategically placed on the field.

reviewer_note: No -ly affix claimed on strategically (strategic + -ally, no 'strategical' base in common use).

corpus_definition: a gentle rub; also a sudden illness affecting the brain

forms.definition: a sudden illness when blood cannot reach part of the brain
forms.example: My grandfather had a stroke and could not speak for a month.

syn.note: A different sudden illness: a heart attack is in the heart, a stroke is in the brain.
A sudden attack of an illness, often with shaking; not the same as a stroke.

forms.definition: to move your hand gently over something many times
forms.example: She stroked the cat's soft fur.
forms.note: Belongs to stroke = a gentle rub with your hand, not the brain illness.
There is no adjective made from stroke.
There is no adverb made from stroke.

context.text: Last year our neighbour had a stroke. Now she goes to a hospital in Tashkent every week, and she is slowly learning to walk again after the stroke.

reviewer_note: CORPUS: one row whose definition mixes two meanings (gentle rub + illness); the example is the illness sense, so the map anchors there and 'gentle rub' is the verb other_meaning. Other stroke meanings (swimming, pen line) not shown.
